newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostages praise Japanese host as crisis hero.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostages praise Japanese host as crisis hero.

text.p: Diplomats and guests released from the Lima hostage crisis praised on Saturday as a hero the host of the ill-fated grand reception that turned to nightmare, Japanse envoy Morihisa Aoki.
Aoki, who early in the ordeal reportedly pleaded with the Marxist guerrillas to release his guests and keep him as the sole captive, was described as brave and caring by freed captives.
The released ambassadors of Brazil, Egypt and South Korea described the veteran diplomat as the "commander of the troops" when they met with Japanese foreign minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Friday.

Japanese officials said the ambassadors recounted the 58- year-old Aoki's level-headed yet caring conduct inside the residence after it was stormed and taken over by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
Aoki never stopped treating his fellow hostages as guests to his quarters, they were quoted as saying.
Luis Martinez, a Jesuit priest who was one of the first to be freed from the siege, was also full of praise for Aoki.

As he addressed a Christmas mass in the city's main plaza on Saturday, Martinez said in Japanese: "Despite the severe situation, the ambassador has shown great calm and bigness of heart. I would like to thank him publicly for the courage he gave to all of us."

In an interview published in the daily El Sol, another released hostage, journalist Manuel Higa called Aoki a "hero," saying that he heard Aoki tell his captors: "Please, no more bullets. These people are my friends. Don't touch them."

Japanese businessman Masazumi Takada, who was also released Friday night, told reporters that Aoki came several times a day to talk to groups of hostages to give them any new information he had, always with an encouraging word.
But even the tireless host -- himself the son of a diplomat -- may be growing weary of the ordeal, now in its fifth day with no early end in sight.
In Saturday evening's dramatic walkie-talkie contact by the guerrillas with Peruvian television, Aoki came on air sounding nervous and inarticulate.
He said in broken Spanish: "It is essential that the Peruvian government and the MRTA promote a peace negotiation."
"In difficult conditions we are well, although there are some ill people," he said.
